meta.title: I2P2: Injury and Illness Prevention Programs
meta.description: Learn how an Injury and Illness Prevention Program helps identify hazards, control risks, train workers, maintain records, and continuously improve workplace safety.

i2p2-overview.title: What Is I2P2?
i2p2-overview.content: An Injury and Illness Prevention Program (I2P2) is an organized, proactive approach to identifying and correcting workplace hazards before injuries or illnesses occur. Rather than reacting after an incident, an effective I2P2 helps employers and employees work together to find hazards, fix unsafe conditions, train workers, and continuously improve the safety program. Core elements include management leadership, employee participation, hazard identification, hazard control, training, recordkeeping, and program evaluation. OSHA's safety and health program guidance describes I2P2 as a proactive way to manage workplace safety and health.
keyPoints: I2P2 focuses on preventing injuries and illnesses rather than reacting to them.
Core elements include hazard identification, hazard control, training, and program evaluation.
Effective programs require both management leadership and employee participation.
Proactive hazard correction protects workers and reduces costly workplace incidents.

management-employee-participation.title: Management Leadership and Employee Participation
management-employee-participation.content: An I2P2 only works when management is visibly committed and employees are actively involved. Management must set safety expectations, assign clear responsibilities, provide adequate resources, communicate openly with workers, and follow through on corrective actions. Employees must report hazards and near misses, follow established safe procedures, participate honestly in training and inspections, and speak up when something looks unsafe. Fear of retaliation for reporting hazards undermines the prevention approach. Supervisors who begin each shift with a safety discussion and encourage open reporting help create a culture where prevention is everyone's responsibility.
keyPoints: Management must set expectations, provide resources, and follow through on corrective actions.
Employees must report hazards, follow safe procedures, and participate in training.
A culture free from retaliation is essential for effective hazard reporting.
Safety cannot succeed if it is treated as only a policy on paper.

hazard-identification.title: Hazard Identification and Assessment
hazard-identification.content: Hazards can be found through workplace inspections, employee reports, near-miss reports, injury and illness records, equipment checks, job hazard analyses, and direct observation of routine tasks. Near misses are especially valuable because they signal that a hazard exists before someone is actually injured. Reporting a hazard is not complaining — it is one of the most important ways employees protect themselves and their coworkers. OSHA Part 1904 injury and illness records can reveal patterns in injury types, departments, tasks, or equipment that point to recurring hazards needing correction.
keyPoints: Hazards are found through inspections, employee reports, near misses, and injury record review.
Near misses warn of hazards before an injury occurs and must be reported.
Reporting hazards is a key employee responsibility under an effective I2P2.
Injury and illness records can reveal recurring patterns that require corrective action.

hazard-prevention-control.title: Hazard Prevention and Control
hazard-prevention-control.content: Once a hazard is identified, the goal is to eliminate or control it using the hierarchy of controls: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment. Engineering controls — such as machine guarding, ventilation, and interlocks — are preferred because they physically remove or reduce the hazard. Administrative controls such as updated procedures, job rotation, and warning systems reduce exposure but do not eliminate the hazard. PPE is important but should not be the only control when more effective options are available. All corrective actions should be documented, assigned to responsible parties, completed on schedule, and verified as effective.
keyPoints: Apply the hierarchy of controls: eliminate, substitute, engineer, administrate, then PPE.
Engineering controls are preferred because they physically remove or reduce the hazard.
PPE alone is not sufficient when engineering or administrative controls are feasible.
Document, assign, and verify corrective actions to ensure they are completed.

education-training.title: Education and Training
education-training.content: Training ensures that employees understand the hazards they face, the procedures that protect them, and their responsibilities for reporting and participation. Training should be provided during new-hire orientation, when job tasks change, when new hazards are introduced, after incidents or near misses, and whenever procedures are updated. Job-specific training that matches actual workplace conditions is more effective than general awareness alone. Training records should be maintained and reviewed as part of the I2P2. A new employee assigned to a chemical area, for example, should receive training on chemical hazards, SDS access, PPE, spill response, and reporting procedures before beginning work.
keyPoints: Training must cover hazards, procedures, responsibilities, and reporting expectations.
Provide training at hire, after incidents, when tasks change, and when new hazards are identified.
Job-specific training matched to real work conditions is most effective.
Training records should be maintained as part of the overall I2P2 documentation.

injury-illness-recordkeeping.title: Injury and Illness Recordkeeping
injury-illness-recordkeeping.content: Under 29 CFR Part 1904, most employers with more than 10 employees must maintain records of occupational injuries and illnesses unless they qualify for an exemption. These records include the OSHA 300 Log, OSHA 301 Incident Report, and OSHA 300A Annual Summary. Recordkeeping requirements also include reporting fatalities and certain severe injuries to OSHA. Beyond compliance, these records are prevention tools. Reviewing injury logs, incident reports, and near-miss data can reveal patterns — repeated hand injuries in one department, for example — that point to specific hazards needing correction. OSHA states that the purpose of Part 1904 is to help identify and eliminate workplace hazards to prevent future incidents.
keyPoints: 29 CFR Part 1904 requires most employers with more than 10 employees to keep injury and illness records.
OSHA forms include the 300 Log, 301 Incident Report, and 300A Annual Summary.
Injury records are not just compliance paperwork — they are hazard prevention tools.
Reviewing records for patterns helps identify recurring hazards needing corrective action.

program-evaluation.title: Program Evaluation and Improvement
program-evaluation.content: An I2P2 must be reviewed and improved over time because workplaces change. Evaluation methods include scheduled inspections, employee feedback, review of incident and near-miss trends, corrective-action tracking, training completion records, and management review sessions. A common program weakness is identifying hazards but not following through on corrective actions. Effective programs assign a responsible person and completion date for each corrective action, then verify that the control is working. The continuous improvement cycle — Plan, Do, Check, Improve — keeps the program aligned with current hazards, procedures, and workforce needs.
keyPoints: Programs must be reviewed and updated as workplace conditions change.
Evaluation tools include inspections, incident trends, employee feedback, and corrective-action tracking.
A frequent weakness is identifying hazards but failing to follow up on corrective actions.
The Plan-Do-Check-Improve cycle drives continuous I2P2 improvement.

Identify and correct hazards before workers are injured or become ill
Provide documentation for lawsuits
Replace other OSHA-required safety programs

False

29 CFR Part 1904

options.text: Remind employees to watch where they walk
Investigate and correct the cause of the slipping hazard
Wait to see if a serious injury occurs before acting

options.text: Telling employees to avoid a dangerous machine instead of repairing it
Relying only on PPE with no other controls in place

They allow supervisors to discipline employees
They replace the need for routine inspections

False

options.text: Only at the time of hire
Only when OSHA issues a citation
During orientation, after incidents, when hazards change, and when procedures are updated

Engineering or administrative controls when feasible
